content: Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW) is an isotopic water standard established in 1968 by the International Atomic Energy Agency. Despite its name, which might suggest a connection to ocean water, VSMOW refers to pure water (H₂O) and does not contain any salts or other substances typically found in seawater. It is primarily used as a reference standard for comparing hydrogen and oxygen isotope ratios, particularly in water samples. Additionally, highly purified and distilled VSMOW water is utilized for precise measurements of water's physical properties and for defining laboratory standards, as it is considered representative of the average water composition on Earth. Historically, average ocean water and melted snow were used as reference points for isotopic measurements. These were refined in the 1960s with the standardized definition of Standard Mean Ocean Water (SMOW). The National Bureau of Standards (now the National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST) developed physical water standards for global use. However, these standards were later questioned. VSMOW was introduced in 1967 as a recalibration of the original SMOW definition. It was created by Harmon Craig and colleagues at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, who mixed distilled ocean waters collected from various locations worldwide. Today, VSMOW remains one of the most widely used isotopic water benchmarks. The isotopic composition of VSMOW is defined as the ratio of the molar abundance of a rare isotope to that of its most common isotope, expressed in parts per million (ppm). For example, the most common oxygen isotope, ¹⁶O (with eight protons and eight neutrons), is approximately 2,632 times more abundant in seawater than the isotope ¹⁷O (which has an additional neutron). This corresponds to a ratio of about 6 ppm (1 part per approximately 2,632 parts). VSMOW is also critical in the production of high-accuracy temperature measurement reference standards. For precise measurements, not all water is suitable due to variations in isotopic composition. Water molecules consist of different isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen, which evaporate at different temperatures and rates. As a result, recently evaporated ocean water, such as snow, river water, and rainwater, tends to be enriched in lighter isotopes that evaporate more quickly. If triple-point-based temperature reference cells are filled with water of improper isotopic composition, errors of several hundred microkelvins can occur in the measured triple point. To address this issue, the International Committee for Weights and Measures (CIPM) affirmed in 2005 that the definition of the Kelvin thermodynamic temperature scale would reference water with an isotopic composition exactly matching the nominal specification of VSMOW. This ensures consistency in defining the triple point of water. The triple point (0.01°C at 611.657 Pa) and the boiling point of water (100°C at 101.325 kPa) are no longer the defining points for the Celsius scale. Instead, the Celsius scale is now defined in terms of the absolute thermodynamic temperature scale, referencing absolute zero and the triple point of water. The difference of approximately 0.000089°C between the original and current definitions of the Celsius scale has minimal practical significance, as water's boiling point is highly sensitive to changes in barometric pressure. For instance, a change in altitude of just 28 cm (11 inches) can alter water's boiling point by one millikelvin. The adoption of the VSMOW standard by the CIPM was based on a recommendation from the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) in their publication Atomic Weights of the Elements: Review 2000.
